speaker: jeremygaston
text: Thank you. And may it please the court, Jeremy Gaston for appellants, Kenneth Lyle and Linda Morrison individually and as trustee of the Ruth Mary Lockhart Trust. This case at bottom is a trespass case. It's a case where one party, Midway Solar, has made such excessive use of the surface of certain property as to block all reasonable access to the minerals that lie underneath that property, minerals owned by appellants, thus constituting trespass in the form of an interference or obstruction or excessive use of surface easement rights and those are the rights that mineral owners have either impliedly or expressly. The ones here are expressed and there are two key issues that I want to focus on. The first is if a mineral owner like appellants finds that their access to the minerals has been blocked by an excessive surface use, must they nevertheless and despite experts saying that there's no reasonable access, must they nevertheless go out and try to access those minerals before they bring a trespass claim for damages in our judicial system? That's the first issue. The second issue is whether the Common Law Accommodation Doctrine applies on any facts as a matter of law across the board to this case based on the 1948 Price Team. Before jumping into the first issue, I'd like to mention a few points as to how we got here. Now, it's a long story in the sense that it dates back 70 years, but there are just a few really key facts to stress. The first is the 1948 Price Deed. In that deed, a group of grantors conveyed thousands of acres of property in West Texas, including the tracted issue here, which is approximately 315 acres in Pecos County. And in conveying that property, they reserved all of the minerals and they expressly reserved a surface easement, giving them the right to use the surface of the property to develop that mineral estate. And they reserved the right specifically to take such, quote, usual, necessary, or convenient actions to develop the mineral estate. And the easement even mentions specifics, such as being able to do all types of geophysical testing, for example. Frankly, though, most of the rights listed in the express easement would also be implied, even if they weren't there under Texas law. The deed also states that the mineral interest owners will have no liability for any damages to the surface or claim damages that have been claimed to result from the usual, necessary, or convenient use of the surface for mineral development. Fast forward 70 years and appellants are now owners with co-tenants of an undivided interest in all the minerals under the tract. And Midway Solar, before this case was filed in 2018, built and completed a solar facility. And the solar energy facility, if you look at it from the sky, almost looks like wall-to-wall carpet of glass. It's contiguous, it occupies 217, approximately 217 out of the 315 acres. And the reason they were able to do that is because they leased the surface of the property from the surface owner, Gary Dergak, and the lease provides them 35 to 55 years of the ability to use the surface. They also got waivers, waivers of the right to use the surface, waivers of the right to use the surface by parties purporting to be owners of minerals under the surface, which, if effective, would have granted Midway the exclusive right to use the surface and not have to worry about mineral development on the surface. However, they didn't get any such waivers from appellants who owned the minerals under the tract. And the waivers they did get were all from parties, 20 parties who don't own any minerals under the tract. The result is a tract of land where 70% is completely covered by solar energy facility solar energy facility, solar panels, and related equipment, leaving 30% at the 5% at the South end and 25% at the North end, theoretically available for mineral development, but as a practical matter, the 5% at the South end is too small to site a well under state rules. And even although the North 25% could be a place to site a well, half of it lies outside of the region that our oil and gas expert said is not the prime area for mineral development. In other words, if you look at a trend of where oil has been discovered in this region, you can trace a line and it goes straight through the center of the solar facility, but it doesn't go through that Northern 25% except part of it. So all told, the vast majority of this land is inaccessible from the surface for oil and gas development. And more particularly, our expert Bill Temple specifically said that because of the geology and economics, you have to access the minerals here vertically through vertical drilling. So you need access to the surface rather than modern forms of horizontal or directional drilling, where you can get to minerals that may be somewhere else by going at a direction or horizontally from the surface of land that's not covered. So that's the situation. And the first issue is if something like that happens, do the affected mineral owners have to nevertheless go out and try and develop the minerals on the property before they can raise a claim in court for damages? Now, our position of course, is that they can come to court and seek damages based on excessive surface use. And to be clear, they don't have, they being appellants, don't have current development activities or plans. And the basis is because they can't, because the surface use by Midway has obstructed that. But the reason they are able to still sue for damages follows from the basic legal principle that property rights are valued and protected, whether you are currently using them or not. And the easy way to see this is to think if the shoe were on the other foot. Suppose mineral owners went to their land where there was say nothing on the surface. And they went there and they dug up the land and they even built a house and things totally unrelated to mineral development activities. Obviously that would be an excessive use of their surface access rights. Does the surface owner, can the surface owner come in and file a claim for trespass based on their excessive use of the surface for damages? Or can the mineral interest say, well, you weren't using it and you don't have any plans to use it. So I can come out and do all of this that is excessive and otherwise unlawful. The answer is the surface owner can sue for damages. And there is no conceptual reason that we look at it differently when it's the mineral interest owner.

speaker: jeffalley
text: I understand, I guess the question I'm asking you and I'll ask Ms. Barron as well. The gist of the Midway's argument seems to be that, okay, wait until you actually try and develop these minerals and at that point, you might be able to bring some sort of claim. And let's say you did that 20 years in the future. And when you did so, would you be subject to a limitations claim on the trespass? Would you be subject to some sort of latches type argument or even an adverse possession claim if you sat here for 20 years and watched all of this go on?

speaker: jeremygaston
text: Right, and certainly we have listed adverse possession as one of the few examples in the law where if you don't use your property rights, you may find that they have been used out from under you, so to speak. And I think latches is a very general doctrine that could apply in numerous circumstances. So I would never rule that out as a conceivable defense. I think if a court said that the litigants here can't seek damages now, then I think it would be hard for a defendant later to raise a limitations claim because the courts have said they can't sue yet. So there would be some tolling I would expect. In this situation, the facility was completed and the suit was filed and so obviously there's not a, well, not briefed or argued yet any limitations issue here. The question you pose, I think, is a good reason that you have to allow the suit now because you don't want situations where someone sits around for 20 years and then raises a claim that could have been made. The answer is when they see the invasion of their property interest, and under Texas law, that would be the basic rule, the legal injury rule. When your property interest has been invaded, then the limitation starts running. That's the general rule, subject to tolling and other exceptions. So here we would say, if there was a limitations clock running, it would start when we were able to bring suit. We believe we were able to bring suit immediately. And that is consistent with the theory that the damages you get are the harm to your mineral interest as of that date of injury. So the value beforehand minus the value afterwards.

speaker: jeffalley
text: And all those- Can I also ask, sorry to interrupt you, but can I also ask, how would you ever prove, if you have no activity where you're seeking leases right now, how would you prove a measure of damage? speaker: jeremygaston
text: Right. So in terms of damages, you could look at it in multiple ways. The people who own the minerals don't have to lease it. They could also develop it themselves. So either way, whether you're looking at the amount of royalties or the amount of bonuses you would get through leasing, or the amount of profits you would make from exploiting it yourself, either of those would be bases for expert testimony where experts would go determine the reserves and the market prices and project it forward or project it in the market. I think the damages analysis would be pretty standard, but I don't think it's good. I don't think this record allows an inference that the appellants aren't in the market for any reason other than they now have an essentially worthless situation where, as our expert said, no reasonably prudent operator would lease the property for mineral purposes. So the situation, in fact, on a damages level would be, what would this property be able to be leased for or what kind of profits could be produced if the facility weren't there or there was reasonable access to the minerals? So back to the point about not being in the market, they're not in the market because they can't be in the market. The market has been taken away from them by the excessive surface use. One of the background principles here is that when parties such as a surface owner and a mineral owner have reciprocal rights, they're both able to use the same property, is the principle that if one uses it excessively to the detriment of the other, they become the trespasser. And that's the Brown versus Lundell case, which we've cited in our reply on page 504. And that really is a fundamental idea as to why you can go forward and seek damages. Now, the alternative, if you propose a rule where a party has to first go out and try and get their minerals, even though experts say it's not feasibly possible, is not only not in any precedent, there's no case saying that you have to have a current use in order to seek damages. And I should be clear about that. There's no case saying you have to have a current use or attempted use in order to seek damages in a trespass case. But the reason not to impose such a hurdle is all you're going to do is both encourage breaches of the peace where someone like appellants goes out with a bulldozer and plans to build an access road through the middle of the solar facility. Obviously there would be an injunction sought, and I'm sure the court would grant an injunction until it could look at the situation better. But if someone is seeking damages for the lost value in their mineral interest, why require the parties to go through injunctions or other outside exercises that are going to be futile? Because remember, at least by assumption, the minerals now are no longer feasibly accessible. So if that is, and if that turns out to be true based on the proof at trial, Midway would owe damages. If it turns out not to be so by the proof, then they wouldn't. But in order to make someone do something futile before they go to court is also not a recognized principle in the law. Even in the context, say, of where people have to seek administrative remedies, there's always futility exceptions. The best case I would say, because this is sort of a case of first impression, but the closest case is the Hopped versus Tarrant County Water Control District, where the Water Control District flooded the surface of property to make a reservoir, and that removed the mineral owner's ability to access their minerals. And the Court of Appeals on remand from the Supreme Court said that unless the Water Control District can prove that these mineral owners still have reasonable access to the minerals, they're gonna owe damages for the value of the unrecoverable minerals. And the evidence, in fact, showed almost conclusively the opposite, the Court of Appeals said. And the only difference between our case and that case, apart from it being glass instead of water, is that there was a government entity as the defendant. And I have heard no argument as to why, whether it's a government entity that has harmed the property interest or a private party that's harmed the property interest, there's gonna be any different analysis. The reason the Supreme Court issued a decision in that case was to say that if the accommodation doctrine applies with respect to the particular actions at issue, then you're gonna use the private law accommodation doctrine not any different standard. So there's no suggestion that there's any different standard. And there shouldn't be, when one party, whether it's the government or private party harms another's property interest, they should be liable for the harm that they caused pursuant to a suit for damages brought to enforce that upon proof that in fact the harm has been caused. The best case for Midway, I would say, is the Lightning Oil case. And as I'll explain, it doesn't fit here, but in that case, Anadarko prepared to drill a eight inch diameter hole across land that was owned by, whose mineral interest was owned by Lightning Oil. And Lightning Oil sought to enjoin Anadarko from drilling that hole based on the idea that it might interfere with their future drilling activities and the Supreme Court said, no, you can't get an injunction based on the speculation that what they do in the future might harm what you might do in the future because that is speculative and not proof of an imminent irreparable harm. Here, however, what's at issue in this appeal is the propriety of being able to seek a damages remedy for the actions, not to enjoin Midway Solar based on actions that have already occurred. Midway has already built the facility. It's not something in the future. And the proof that it has caused harm is not speculative. It was given with two expert affidavits and none of that was factually controverted. And I should mention as a fourth point, it's even on its face, the idea that a eight inch diameter hole across some land is a far cry from a 217 acre facility that completely covers the land. And more generally, cases like lightning oil do show that when you're not currently engaged in a competing use, or you don't have a plan for that immediately, injunctive relief is going to be probably not available. It just doesn't meet the standard for an injunction. But the standard for damages is, have you proven by preponderance of the evidence or here more than a scintilla, cause we're at summary judgment. Have you proven that there's been a harm to your property interest? And if so, what's the value of it? Against all of this Midway's one response is that this is an accommodation doctrine case and accommodation doctrine cases require a current competing use. But this is not an accommodation case. We don't have a current competing use. We are not seeking to have competing uses accommodated. We're seeking to have damages remedy and whether or not the accommodation doctrine applies, I think the basic principle, and you could sum up this case in this one sentence, you can't block someone from being able to exercise their rights and then say they can't complain about it because they're not exercising their rights. That's a catch 22 and it is not necessary to impose.

speaker: jeremygaston
text: Yes. In their motion for traditional summary judgment, which was their third motion, they asked that their actions be declared reasonable as a matter of law. They didn't submit any evidence in support of that motion. And because the mineral deed here reserves the right to conduct usual activities, even if they are unnecessary or inconvenient, that would be an example where the deed shows that the accommodation doctrine can't apply, at least as between vertical and horizontal drilling, even in theory, it might apply for other choices. But that shows why it's a difficult issue to get into and why we would say it's probably an advisory opinion to try and rule that it can or can't apply across the board as a matter of law right now. I know I'm out of my opening time, so.

speaker: jeffalley
text: Thank you, council. Ms. Barron.

speaker: pamelabaron
text: May it please court. A lot of appellants are asking this court to go where no court has ever gone before, to be the first court in Texas to recognize a cause of action for damages by a mineral owner complaining about how a landowner is going about using his land when the mineral owner is not currently developing and has no plan to develop the minerals. And the court should reject this for three reasons and affirm the summary judgment on the breach of contract and trespass claims. And let me give you the executive summary of those three reasons first. The first is there's no remedy without a right. And what the right they're arguing for here is contrary to the express terms of the 1948 D. It says you can only use the surface in conjunction with use of the minerals. They've conceded they're not engaging in use. The second thing is their argument conflicts with, and it's based on a fundamental misunderstanding of the accommodation doctrine. Under the accommodation doctrine, the minerals are always accessible. The end game there is not damages, it is development. So we wanna maximize, we wanna encourage maximum use of the surface when there's a conflict between severed estates. And so how that works is if the land owner doesn't meet its showing, then they have to yield and mineral development goes forward as planned. But if they do, mineral development still goes forward just in a slightly altered form that permits the existing surface use. So the end result is always development of the minerals. Access to the minerals is not lost, but you don't get damages. And then the third point is what they're arguing for has no support in Texas law. They're relying on the Hopped case. They're saying that's the closest thing they've got. I'll go into it more in detail in the body of my argument, but the two important distinctions up front are, there there was very active mineral development, not idle mineral owners like we have here. And second, it's a world of difference between a tort action or a breach of contract action against a private land owner and an inverse condemnation action against a governmental entity. If a governmental entity can't meet its showing under the accommodation doctrine and would normally be required to yield, it has an option that a private land owner doesn't have. It can say no, it can block development to protect the public interest, there to protect the public water supply. But if it does that, it pays damages, not a breach of contract or some common law action, but under the Texas constitution, article one, section 17. So my plan is to just expand on those three points, but let me start by saying, you know, trespass, we're start, they have the cart before the horse. You gotta start, you have to have a right before you get damages. And the right they claim here either has to come from the 1948 deed or the accommodation doctrine. And first of all, it doesn't come from the 1948 deed. As we just said, Mr. Durgac is the land owner under the 1948 deed, he has a hundred percent fee simple interest in section 14. He lives on the North half, he leaves the South half to Midway for solar development. And the Lyles are claiming that they own part of the mineral interest under section 14, both the North and South halves. And as you just heard them say, it's undisputed, they're not currently using the minerals, they don't have any plans to use them. Any right they may have has to come by their reservation of the mineral interest in the 1948 deed. And in Texas, we don't imply rights under a reservation in a deed. That's the Perryman case in the Texas Supreme Court in 2018. It has to be expressed, it has to be out there in black and white.

speaker: jeffalley
text: And they're saying- Ms. Barron, excuse me. How do you answer the kind of, what I would call the chicken and the egg argument? That their argument that I can't lease this property, I can't develop it because, you know, any land man who went out there and looked at it would say, it's 70% covered by these solar panels and I don't wanna fool with trying to decide where I can drill or horizontally drill.

speaker: pamelabaron
text: Well, first they'd have to have the right to exclude Mr. Durgat from using his land as he sees fit. And then Lightning also rejected that where they said Lightning was arguing that it should have the right to prevent any surface use that might later interfere with its plans. And the Supreme Court said, no, we're not gonna change oil and gas in such a radical way. But the other point is that's how the accommodation doctrine works. As the Supreme Court's recognized, it's been tried and true for more than 50 years. These situations work themselves out. The developer comes in, they may put the stakes down where they're gonna put their drill pad. The landowner objects, they either work it out amicably or they do it through an injunction. But in terms of their no liability provision, that's the common law in Texas. A mineral owner does not have liability to the surface owner for surface damage in conjunction with developing the minerals, unless there's some specific agreement between the parties. And the Texas Supreme Court realized this. I mean, that was from the Humble Oil case in 1967. And Getty Oil was the big accommodation case 40 years later. So the accommodation doctrine was adopted with the background of knowing that the mineral owner is not responsible for damage to the surface estate. So let me expand a little bit on Getty Oil because the accommodation doctrine really is bedrock law in Texas. Getty Oil came out in 1971. Three takeaways are very important in that case that are relevant here. First, what I said at the beginning is that the minerals are always accessible. The end game of the accommodation doctrine is not damages, it's mineral development in one form or another. The second takeaway is the size of the project doesn't matter. They're saying we use 215 out of the 315 acres for the solar farm, but in Getty, it was even more extensive. There, the irrigation system covered almost the entire 128 acre tract, as the court noted in its opinion, except for a few corner areas. And the court said the accommodation doctrine applies no matter if it's sparsely developed, like open prairie land for grazing, or whether it's densely developed. And they gave some good examples. They said the accommodation doctrine applies to a residential area in the city of Houston. It applies to the UT Austin campus. It applies to cities, parks, lakes, prison lands, and industrial sites. So the size of the project has nothing to do with whether the accommodation doctrine doesn't come in and resolve the dispute so that we can maximize use of the surface between competing estates. At the end of the day, there is going to be use and there is access to the minerals. And then the third thing I wanna say about Getty is yeah, it has to be same place, same time. And that's built into the elements. This court had an opinion on the accommodation doctrine in 2018. Justice Rodriguez wrote the opinion for the court in Harrison versus Rosetta resources. And in reciting the standard, you said that the first showing is that the surface owner has to show that the mineral owner's use of the surface or the mineral owner's activities on the surface are impeding existing use. So you can't get there until there's actual use and actual activities by the mineral owner on the surface. And Lightning Oil said that too. It said, you can't complain now. The accommodation doctrine tried and true. We'll take care of that if there's a conflict in the future on how and where wells or well pads will be located on the site. And then-

speaker: jeffalley

speaker: pamelabaron
text: None. There are none, because they own the mineral interest. They have the right to use the mineral interest. That doesn't change under the 1948 deed. And the accommodation doctrine, as the Supreme Court said, will take care of it when we get there. text: Yes, Your Honor, thank you. I think it is the chicken and egg question here. And although the accommodation doctrine has been around a very long time, damages remedies for trespass have been around even longer. And the case law that we cite indicates that property rights, such as a surface easement are valuable and protectable. And apart from certain circumstances like adverse possession, don't require you to use them. These property rights could be bought or sold or leased or developed. There are many ways in which they have value. And when another party, in this case, the one who's able to exercise the rights of the servient estate, so the Midway Solar operating on the surface is the servient estate to appellants who are the dominant state with respect to the surface easement that they have. This is just a quote from the Severance versus Patterson case from the Texas Supreme Court in 2012. We cited a reply brief at page 18, note 46. Because the easement holder is the dominant estate owner and the land burdened by the easement is the servient estate, the property owner may not interfere with the easement holder's right to use the servient estate for the purposes of the easement. Suppose the surface estate had just built, suppose there are some roads on the surface estate and the surface owner had put trucks all along the roads. And suppose someone had a surface easement and they had the right to use the road to get from A to B on the land. But now they can't because it's blocked by all these trucks. Do they have to try and go through the trucks? Do they have to do anything? Can they, I mean, they might make a phone call and say, would you please move your trucks? And maybe they say yes, maybe they say no. Or can they file a lawsuit and seek damages for interference with their right? And if property rights only have value and are only protected when they are being affirmatively used, that would be one thing. But maybe an easiest way to see it, suppose the solar facility, instead of taking up 70% of the tract and leaving 5% unusable and what was remaining with the surface area open was not in the most desirable. I mean, that's our situation. Suppose it had covered 99.9% of the tract. And suppose it had covered it with 30 feet blocks of asphalt to where it's so obvious you can't do anything here. Do they still have to go out and try? In our opinion, that's just a matter of degree. It's gonna be far easier for that party to show that there has been an excessive surface use than someone where only 85 or 75% of the tract is unavailable or undesirable, which would still be easier than someone who say it only covered 15% of the tract. Those are matters of degree. Conceptually though, under Midway's argument, even if the entire tract was completely covered in 30 feet of concrete, you still can't say my property rights have been trampled on. You have to try and use them, even though no one would even be able to give you a way to try and use them. Here, experts have said it's not feasible to go out there and try and get the minerals. They are valueless. They can't be leased. They can't be exercised. And so it is, it is a chicken and egg. If someone can come around and cross over your property rights and their excuse is, well, you weren't using them. And even though you now can't use them, you just have no remedy. We did have a right. We had the reserved right to use the surface for such purposes as are usual, necessary or convenient in the development of the mineral state. And now the experts say that right is valueless. And so it is futile. And while there may not be a case involving this situation, it's the rare situation where the entirety of a surface has been completely blocked for a contiguous acreage, which is why this is a case of first impression in that regard. One, an example, they say we don't have any damages and we don't have any rights. As a mineral owner, we have the right to pick where to put our wells.
